topic: Mastering Binomial Distributions: From Coin Flips to Success

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Bernoulli Trial
sections.content: Define a Bernoulli trial as an experiment with exactly two outcomes (Success/Failure) and a constant probability 'p'. Visualize this as a single path split in a decision tree.
sections.example: A smart-home sensor checking if a door is 'Locked' (p=0.8) or 'Unlocked' (q=0.2).

sections.title: Defining the Binomial Distribution
sections.content: Introduce the B(n, p) notation. Explain the four requirements (BINS): Binary outcomes, Independent trials, Number of trials is fixed, and Success probability is constant.
sections.example: A squirrel gathering 10 nuts; each nut has a 50% chance of being an acorn. n=10, p=0.5.

sections.title: The Binomial Formula: The Logic of Combinations
sections.content: Break down the formula P(X=k) = C(n,k) * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k). Explain that C(n,k) counts the ways to arrange 'k' successes, and p^k(1-p)^(n-k) defines the probability of one specific sequence.
sections.example: Visualizing a probability histogram where the bars show the likelihood of getting exactly 0 to 10 successes, forming the characteristic 'bell-like' shape.

sections.title: Application: The Robot Quality Control
sections.content: Calculate the probability of exactly 3 successes in 5 trials using the formula. Demonstrate how changing 'p' shifts the center of gravity of the distribution graph.
sections.example: A factory robot inspects 5 microchips. If each chip has a 10% defect rate (failure), what is the probability of finding exactly 1 defective chip?

sections.title: Summary & Real-World Utility
sections.content: Recap the mean (np) and variance (npq). Briefly mention how this distribution acts as a foundation for hypothesis testing and predicting rare events.
sections.example: Predicting the number of successful deliveries a drone makes in a fleet of 50, given a known success rate per flight.
